```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)
library(tidyr)

theme_set(theme_bw())

timings <- readRDS("results/timings.rds")
monitors <- readRDS("results/monitors.rds")
meta <- readRDS("results/meta.rds")

workers <- meta$workers

wl_label <- c(
  boot_metrics = "A: Bootstrap metrics",
  resample_fit = "B: Resampled model fits",
  perm_importance = "C: Permutation importance",
  boot_pred_interval = "D: Bootstrap prediction intervals"
)

backend_label <- c(
  sequential = "sequential",
  future = "future (multisession)",
  mirai = "mirai",
  mizu = "mizu",
  mizu_stream = "mizu (stream)"
)

backend_cols <- c(
  "future (multisession)" = "#7570B3",
  "mirai" = "#1B9E77",
  "mizu" = "#E7298A",
  "mizu (stream)" = "#F49EC4"
)

bench <- timings |>
  mutate(
    workload = wl_label[workload],
    backend = backend_label[backend]
  )

baseline <- bench |>
  filter(backend == "sequential") |>
  summarize(baseline = mean(elapsed), .by = workload)

par_bench <- bench |>
  filter(backend != "sequential") |>
  inner_join(baseline, by = "workload") |>
  mutate(
    speed_up = baseline / elapsed,
    workload = factor(workload, levels = wl_label),
    backend = factor(backend, levels = backend_label)
  )

# Timing statistics use the three timed runs; the syrup-monitored run
# (which pays the sampler's overhead) is excluded, but is still plotted.
summ <- par_bench |>
  filter(!monitored) |>
  summarize(
    runs = n(),
    mean_elapsed = mean(elapsed),
    sd_elapsed = sd(elapsed),
    mean_speedup = mean(speed_up),
    efficiency = mean_speedup / workers,
    .by = c(workload, backend)
  ) |>
  arrange(workload, desc(mean_speedup))

mon_all <- monitors |>
  mutate(
    workload = wl_label[workload],
    backend = backend_label[backend]
  ) |>
  mutate(rel_time = as.numeric(time - min(time)), .by = c(workload, backend))

mon <- mon_all |>
  filter(pid != main_pid)

busy <- mon |>
  summarize(cores = sum(pct_cpu) / 100, .by = c(workload, backend, rel_time)) |>
  mutate(
    workload = factor(workload, levels = wl_label),
    backend = factor(backend, levels = backend_label)
  )

fmt <- function(x, d = 1) formatC(x, digits = d, format = "f")

get_speedup <- function(wl, be) {
  summ |>
    filter(workload == wl_label[[wl]], backend == backend_label[[be]]) |>
    pull(mean_speedup)
}
get_elapsed <- function(wl, be) {
  summ |>
    filter(workload == wl_label[[wl]], backend == backend_label[[be]]) |>
    pull(mean_elapsed)
}
```

## Overview

Resampling is the expensive part of most modeling work. A bootstrap or
cross-validation run fits the same model hundreds of times. On one core
this takes minutes or hours. Parallel workers cut this to a fraction of
the time.

Several backends can supply those workers, and they are not equally
fast. This report compares three of them — **future**, **mirai**, and
**mizu** — on four modeling workloads built from tidymodels packages.
The workloads are common modeling tasks: bootstrap confidence intervals,
resampled model fits, permutation importance, and bootstrap prediction
intervals. They also move increasing amounts of data between the main
session and the workers, which is where the backends differ most.

Every workload also runs sequentially, as a baseline and as a
correctness reference: each backend must return results identical to
the sequential run.[^method] All runs use `r workers` workers on a
`r meta$cores`-core Apple Silicon Mac
(R `r sub("R version ", "", meta$r_version)`).

[^method]: This report extends the methodology of
    [topepo/bootstrap-parallel-benchmark](https://github.com/topepo/bootstrap-parallel-benchmark).
    Each backend runs each workload once as a warmup (which is also the
    correctness check), three times timed, and once under a CPU monitor.
    The monitor samples the worker processes with
    [syrup](https://github.com/simonpcouch/syrup) at a 50 ms target
    interval (about 5 Hz realized, because each `ps` snapshot costs
    about 0.15 s). The timing statistics use the three unmonitored runs.
    The monitored run appears in the figures only.

## The workloads

Each workload is a standard modeling task, sized so that a sequential
run takes a few minutes:

- **A: Bootstrap metrics.** Compute bootstrap confidence intervals for
  the performance of a regression model: score 5,000 bootstrap splits
  with four yardstick metrics (`rmse`, `rsq`, `mae`, `ccc`).
- **B: Resampled model fits.** The same pattern as `fit_resamples()`:
  fit a workflow (a recipe plus logistic regression) on 250 bootstrap
  resamples, and score each fit on its held-out rows.
- **C: Permutation importance.** Measure how much each predictor
  matters to a fitted model. On 240 bootstrap replicates of a
  validation set, permute each of the 30 predictors in turn and record
  the drop in AUC.
- **D: Bootstrap prediction intervals.** Quantify the uncertainty of
  expected losses for a book of insurance policies. Each task refits a
  Gamma severity model on one of 400 bootstrap splits and scores all
  250,000 policies.

```{r}
#| label: workload-table

tibble(
  Workload = unname(wl_label),
  `What it represents` = c(
    "bootstrap confidence intervals with yardstick metric sets",
    "fit_resamples() on a parsnip workflow (recipe + logistic regression)",
    "bootstrap permutation importance: 240 replicates, each permuting all 30 predictors in turn",
    "bootstrap prediction intervals: refit a Gamma severity model, score the whole portfolio"
  ),
  Tasks = as.integer(meta$n_tasks[names(wl_label)]),
  `Per-task cost` = c("~3 ms", "~45 ms", "~85 ms", "~90 ms"),
  `Per-task input` = c(
    "1 bootstrap split (~200 KB)",
    "1 bootstrap split (~1.7 MB)",
    "1 bootstrap replicate (~2.8 MB)",
    "1 bootstrap split (~3.4 MB)"
  ),
  `Shared input (constant)` = c(
    "—",
    "—",
    "fitted glm (0.2 MB)",
    "38 MB portfolio (250k policies)"
  ),
  `Per-task result` = c(
    "4-row tibble",
    "2-row tibble",
    "30-row tibble",
    "250k-length numeric (2 MB)"
  )
) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

The workloads grow heavier in data terms from A to D: larger per-task
inputs, then a large shared input, then large per-task results. Each
task function loads its own packages with `require()`, so every backend
pays the same worker setup cost.[^tasks]

[^tasks]: No backend-specific export mechanism is used. future's globals
    export, mirai's `.args`, and mizu's staging all carry the same data.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The exact task functions

```r
# A: yardstick metrics on one bootstrap split
task_metrics <- function(split) {
  require(rsample)
  require(yardstick)
  mtr <- metric_set(rmse, rsq, mae, ccc)
  mtr(analysis(split), y, .pred)
}

# B: parsnip workflow fit on the analysis set, scored out-of-bag
task_fit_glm <- function(split) {
  require(rsample); require(recipes); require(parsnip)
  require(workflows); require(yardstick); require(dplyr)
  wf <- workflow() |>
    add_recipe(recipe(class ~ ., data = analysis(split)) |>
                 step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())) |>
    add_model(logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm"))
  fitted <- fit(wf, data = analysis(split))
  assess <- assessment(split)
  pred <- predict(fitted, assess, type = "prob") |>
    bind_cols(predict(fitted, assess, type = "class")) |>
    bind_cols(assess |> select(class))
  bind_rows(roc_auc(pred, class, .pred_yes),
            accuracy(pred, class, .pred_class))
}

# C: one bootstrap replicate of the validation set; permute each
# predictor in turn and record the AUC drop against the pre-fit model
task_permimp <- function(task, model) {
  require(rsample); require(yardstick); require(dplyr)
  set.seed(task$seed, kind = "Mersenne-Twister")
  dat <- analysis(task$split)
  truth <- dat$y
  pred <- as.numeric(predict(model, newdata = dat, type = "response"))
  base_auc <- roc_auc_vec(truth, pred, event_level = "second")
  cols <- setdiff(colnames(dat), "y")
  importance <- numeric(length(cols))
  for (j in seq_along(cols)) {
    orig <- dat[[cols[j]]]
    dat[[cols[j]]] <- orig[sample.int(length(orig))]
    p <- as.numeric(predict(model, newdata = dat, type = "response"))
    importance[j] <- base_auc - roc_auc_vec(truth, p, event_level = "second")
    dat[[cols[j]]] <- orig
  }
  tibble(col = cols, base_auc = base_auc, importance = importance)
}

# D: refit the severity model on one bootstrap split and predict
# expected loss for every policy in the shared portfolio
task_bootpred <- function(split, portfolio) {
  require(rsample)
  fit <- glm(loss ~ ., data = analysis(split),
             family = Gamma(link = "log"), control = list(maxit = 25))
  as.numeric(predict(fit, newdata = portfolio, type = "response"))
}
```
:::

## The three backends

All three backends run the same operation: apply a task function to
every task, then collect the results. They differ in how data moves
between the main R session and the workers.[^transport]

- **future** (multisession, via future.apply) splits the task list into
  one chunk per worker and sends the chunks over sockets, one after
  another.
- **mirai** keeps a pool of persistent workers and streams tasks to
  them over sockets as they become free.
- **mizu** keeps a pool of workers that share memory with the main
  session. The inputs are written once, every worker reads the same
  copy, and the results come back through the same shared
  memory.[^mizu-status]

The worker pools are created once per backend, outside the timed
region.[^calls]

[^transport]: The mechanics matter because copying dominates when tasks
    carry data. future serializes each worker's chunk once per call.
    mirai serializes one payload per task. mizu stages the inputs once
    per call into shared memory; the workers read the same physical
    pages and publish their results there, and the main session reads
    those results as zero-copy views. Workload D also runs a streaming
    mizu variant, `mizu_map(..., .stream = TRUE)`, which sends the task
    list to the workers in slices under a sliding window instead of
    staging it all at once. This is the same per-chunk transport model
    as mirai, but the results still cross as zero-copy views.

[^mizu-status]: mizu is experimental and not yet on CRAN. Install it
    with `pak::pak("shikokuchuo/mizu")`.

[^calls]: The setup is `plan(multisession, workers = 12)`,
    `daemons(12)`, or `mizu_pool(12)`. The timed calls are
    `future.apply::future_lapply(tasks, fn, portfolio = portfolio)`,
    `mirai::mirai_map(tasks, fn, .args = list(portfolio = portfolio))[]`,
    and
    `mizu::mizu_map(pool, tasks, fn, portfolio = portfolio) |> mizu::mizu_collect()`.
    Workload D passes its 38 MB portfolio as a constant argument through
    each backend's natural map call. mizu's map is two-phase:
    `mizu_map()` stages and submits the work, and `mizu_collect()`
    waits for the gathered results (mirai's `[]` collect has the same
    two-phase shape). Both halves sit inside the timed region, so the
    measured work matches the blocking maps of the other backends.

## Results

Every backend returned results identical to the sequential reference
(`all.equal()` at 1e-8 tolerance) for all four workloads:
`r if (all(unlist(meta$correct))) paste("all", length(meta$correct), "backend × workload combinations match.") else paste("MISMATCH:", names(meta$correct)[!unlist(meta$correct)])`

```{r}
#| label: results-table

summ |>
  mutate(
    elapsed = sprintf("%.2f ± %.2f", mean_elapsed, sd_elapsed),
    speedup = fmt(mean_speedup, 2),
    efficiency = fmt(100 * efficiency, 0)
  ) |>
  select(
    Workload = workload, Backend = backend, Runs = runs,
    `Elapsed (s)` = elapsed, `Speed-up` = speedup,
    `Efficiency (%)` = efficiency
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "llrrrr")
```

```{r}
#| label: speedups
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5

ggplot(par_bench, aes(backend, speed_up, col = backend)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, lty = 2, col = "red") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = workers, lty = 2, col = "darkgreen") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.08, alpha = 3 / 4, cex = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~workload) +
  scale_color_manual(values = backend_cols) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Speed-up vs sequential", col = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", axis.text.x = element_blank())
```

Each point is one run. The dashed lines mark no speed-up (red) and
perfect scaling on `r workers` workers (green). The pattern is the same
on all four workloads:

1. **mizu is the fastest backend everywhere**, in both of its
   configurations on workload D.
2. **mirai is second everywhere.**
3. **future falls further behind as tasks carry more data.** On
   workloads A and D it is slower than running sequentially.

## How well do the backends scale?

Adding workers helps only up to a point. Amdahl's law says that the
ceiling on the speed-up is set by the share of the work that stays
serial.[^amdahl] The figure below inverts the law at each measured
`r workers`-worker speed-up. Each curve passes through the mean of its
measured points by construction, so the content of the plot is the
shape: what more workers would buy if the serial share stayed constant.

[^amdahl]: Amdahl's law gives the speed-up from a workload with
    parallel fraction $p$ on $n$ workers as
    $S(n) = 1 / ((1 - p) + p / n)$. This saturates at $1 / (1 - p)$ as
    $n$ grows: the serial fraction, not the worker count, sets the
    ceiling. Inverting the law at a measured speed-up gives the
    *implied* parallel fraction of a backend and workload:
    $p = (1 - 1/S) / (1 - 1/n)$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Amdahl's law reference curves

```{r}
#| label: amdahl-reference
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5

amdahl <- function(n, p) 1 / ((1 - p) + p / n)

expand_grid(n = seq(1, 24, by = 0.25), p = c(0.5, 0.75, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99)) |>
  mutate(speedup = amdahl(n, p), frac = paste0(100 * p, "%")) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, speedup, col = frac)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 22, y = 22.8, label = "ideal (S = n)", col = "grey40") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 6, 12, 18, 24)) +
  labs(x = "workers", y = "speed-up", col = "parallel fraction") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: amdahl-fits
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6

fits <- summ |>
  mutate(
    p = (1 - 1 / mean_speedup) / (1 - 1 / workers),
    max_speedup = 1 / (1 - p)
  )

imp_serial <- function(wl, be) {
  p <- fits |>
    filter(workload == wl_label[[wl]], backend == backend_label[[be]]) |>
    pull(p)
  100 * (1 - p)
}

curves <- fits |>
  reframe(tibble(n = seq(1, 24, by = 0.25)), .by = c(workload, backend, p)) |>
  mutate(speedup = amdahl(n, p))

labels <- fits |>
  mutate(
    speedup = amdahl(24, p),
    lab = ifelse(
      p >= 0,
      sprintf("%s: %.0f%% parallel (max %.1f×)", backend, 100 * p, max_speedup),
      sprintf("%s: p < 0 (slowdown)", backend)
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(workload, desc(speedup)) |>
  mutate(vj = rep(c(1.4, -0.6), length.out = n()), .by = workload)

ggplot(curves, aes(n, speedup, col = backend)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(
    data = par_bench, aes(workers, speed_up), alpha = 3 / 4, cex = 1.5,
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, seed = 1)
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = labels,
    aes(24, speedup, label = lab, col = backend, vjust = vj),
    hjust = 1, size = 2.6, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~workload) +
  scale_color_manual(values = backend_cols) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 6, 12, 18, 24)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.08))) +
  labs(x = "workers", y = "speed-up vs sequential", col = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

- **mizu** is still climbing at `r workers` workers on A, B, and C. The
  implied serial shares are
  `r fmt(imp_serial("boot_metrics", "mizu"), 0)`% on A,
  `r fmt(imp_serial("resample_fit", "mizu"), 0)`% on B, and
  `r fmt(imp_serial("perm_importance", "mizu"), 0)`% on C.
- **mirai** is still climbing on C. On A and D it is at its ceiling,
  where per-task copying dominates.
- **future** speeds up by less than 1 on A and D, which the law cannot
  express. The model assumes a fixed serial share, but future's
  dispatch overhead grows with the worker count (see CPU utilization).
  The flat curves there are a symptom of that overhead, not a
  prediction.

### Checking the fit with a worker sweep

The curves above are extrapolations from a single measurement at
`r workers` workers. As a check, workloads B and C were re-run at 2, 4,
and 8 workers per backend.[^sweep] The solid lines join the measured
mean speed-ups. The dotted curves are the Amdahl predictions pinned at
each backend's 12-worker mean. Everything left of 12 is the model
predicting runs it had not seen.

[^sweep]: Run with `BENCH_SWEEP=1 Rscript benchmark.R`: the same task
    sets, three timed runs per point, and the sequential baseline
    re-measured in the same session.

```{r}
#| label: amdahl-sweep
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5

sweep_raw <- readRDS("results/sweep.rds")

sweep <- sweep_raw$timings |>
  mutate(
    workload = wl_label[workload],
    backend = backend_label[backend]
  )

sweep_base <- sweep |>
  filter(backend == "sequential") |>
  summarize(baseline = mean(elapsed), .by = workload)

sweep_meas <- sweep |>
  filter(backend != "sequential") |>
  inner_join(sweep_base, by = "workload") |>
  mutate(
    speed_up = baseline / elapsed,
    workload = factor(workload, levels = wl_label),
    backend = factor(backend, levels = backend_label)
  )

sweep_n <- max(sweep$workers)

# Amdahl prediction pinned at each backend's mean 12-worker speed-up
sweep_pred <- sweep_meas |>
  filter(workers == sweep_n) |>
  summarize(s_top = mean(speed_up), .by = c(workload, backend)) |>
  mutate(p = (1 - 1 / s_top) / (1 - 1 / sweep_n)) |>
  reframe(
    tibble(n = seq(1, sweep_n, by = 0.25)),
    .by = c(workload, backend, p)
  ) |>
  mutate(speedup = amdahl(n, p))

# Karp-Flatt: the implied serial fraction at each worker count —
# constant under Amdahl, drifting when overhead grows with workers
kf <- sweep_meas |>
  summarize(s = mean(speed_up), .by = c(workload, backend, workers)) |>
  mutate(serial = 100 * (1 - (1 - 1 / s) / (1 - 1 / workers)))

kf_serial <- function(wl, be, w) {
  kf |>
    filter(
      workload == wl_label[[wl]],
      backend == backend_label[[be]],
      workers == w
    ) |>
    pull(serial)
}
kf_s <- function(wl, be, w) {
  kf |>
    filter(
      workload == wl_label[[wl]],
      backend == backend_label[[be]],
      workers == w
    ) |>
    pull(s)
}
kf_range <- function(wl, be, w) {
  d <- sweep_meas |>
    filter(
      workload == wl_label[[wl]],
      backend == backend_label[[be]],
      workers == w
    ) |>
    pull(speed_up)
  c(min(d), max(d))
}

ggplot(sweep_meas, aes(workers, speed_up, col = backend)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey50") +
  geom_line(data = sweep_pred, aes(n, speedup), lty = 3, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 1 / 2, cex = 1.2,
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, seed = 1)
  ) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line", linewidth = 0.8) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", cex = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~workload) +
  scale_color_manual(values = backend_cols) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2, 4, 8, 12)) +
  labs(x = "workers", y = "speed-up vs sequential", col = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Every backend × worker count returned results identical to the
sequential reference
(`r if (all(unlist(sweep_raw$correct))) "all 24 combinations match" else paste("MISMATCH:", names(sweep_raw$correct)[!unlist(sweep_raw$correct)])`).

If the law held exactly, the implied serial share would be the same at
every worker count. Its drift across 2, 4, 8, and 12 workers is the
diagnostic.[^karpflatt] Measured:

- **mizu** — near-flat:
  `r fmt(kf_serial("resample_fit", "mizu", 2), 1)`→`r fmt(kf_serial("resample_fit", "mizu", 12), 1)`%
  on B,
  `r fmt(kf_serial("perm_importance", "mizu", 2), 1)`→`r fmt(kf_serial("perm_importance", "mizu", 12), 1)`%
  on C. The measured points track the fitted curve closely, so mizu's
  curves in the previous figure mean what they say.
- **mirai** — the share *falls* as workers increase (B:
  `r fmt(kf_serial("resample_fit", "mirai", 2), 0)`→`r fmt(kf_serial("resample_fit", "mirai", 12), 0)`%,
  C:
  `r fmt(kf_serial("perm_importance", "mirai", 2), 0)`→`r fmt(kf_serial("perm_importance", "mirai", 12), 0)`%).
  Per-task copying hurts most at 2 workers, where B barely speeds up at
  all (`r fmt(kf_s("resample_fit", "mirai", 2), 1)`×), and the cost
  amortizes as more workers join. The 12-pinned curve over-promises at
  2–4 workers.
- **future** — the share *rises* with workers (B:
  `r fmt(kf_serial("resample_fit", "future", 2), 0)`→`r fmt(kf_serial("resample_fit", "future", 12), 0)`%,
  C:
  `r fmt(kf_serial("perm_importance", "future", 2), 0)`→`r fmt(kf_serial("perm_importance", "future", 12), 0)`%).
  The measured speed-up peaks at 4–8 workers
  (`r fmt(kf_s("resample_fit", "future", 4), 1)`–`r fmt(kf_s("perm_importance", "future", 8), 1)`×)
  and declines by 12, as the dispatch overhead costs more than the
  added workers return. future's 12-worker runs are also the most
  variable in the benchmark: on C alone they span
  `r fmt(kf_range("perm_importance", "future", 12)[1], 1)`–`r fmt(kf_range("perm_importance", "future", 12)[2], 1)`×
  (a
  `r round(100 * (kf_range("perm_importance", "future", 12)[2] / kf_range("perm_importance", "future", 12)[1] - 1))`%
  spread), where mirai and mizu stay within single digits.

The net: trust the fitted curves for mizu on both workloads, and for
mirai on C from about 8 workers up. Everywhere else, the measured
points, not the curves, are the scaling story.

[^karpflatt]: The implied serial share at each worker count is the
    Karp–Flatt metric. A constant value means Amdahl's assumption
    holds. A rising value means the overhead grows with the worker
    count, and a falling value means the overhead amortizes.

## CPU utilization

The monitor recorded how many worker cores were busy through each
monitored run:

```{r}
#| label: cpu-aggregate
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5

ggplot(busy, aes(rel_time, cores, col = backend)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = workers, lty = 2, col = "darkgreen") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~workload, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_color_manual(values = backend_cols) +
  labs(x = "seconds into run", y = "busy worker cores", col = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

mirai and mizu keep their workers busy on A, B, and C. future does
not, and on D the mirai workers stall for long stretches. Two patterns
explain the gaps.

```{r}
#| label: anomalies-data
#| include: false

cores_mean <- busy |>
  summarize(mean_cores = mean(cores), .by = c(workload, backend))

mc <- function(wl, be) {
  cores_mean |>
    filter(workload == wl_label[[wl]], backend == backend_label[[be]]) |>
    pull(mean_cores)
}
# kernel CPU-seconds per wall-clock second, main process (unmonitored runs)
sysr <- function(wl, be) {
  d <- timings[
    timings$workload == wl & timings$backend == be & !timings$monitored,
  ]
  mean(d$system / d$elapsed)
}
```

**future makes its workers wait in line.** The main session prepares
one chunk per worker and sends the chunks one at a time, so a worker
stays idle until its chunk has fully arrived. On workload A, future's
workers average only `r fmt(mc("boot_metrics", "future"), 1)` of
`r workers` cores busy (B: `r fmt(mc("resample_fit", "future"), 1)`),
where mirai and mizu sustain `r fmt(mc("boot_metrics", "mirai"), 1)`
and `r fmt(mc("boot_metrics", "mizu"), 1)`. This is why future's
speed-ups in A and B fall so far short despite 12 workers.[^chunks]

**On workload D, mirai's main session does the heavy lifting.** mirai
sends the shared portfolio with every task, so the main session spends
the run serializing about 17 GB of payloads while the workers average
`r fmt(mc("boot_pred_interval", "mirai"), 1)` of `r workers` cores.
mizu writes the portfolio once, and its workers sustain
`r fmt(mc("boot_pred_interval", "mizu"), 1)` cores.[^sysr]

[^chunks]: The per-worker grids show the effect as a saw-tooth: 1–2 s
    bursts of activity that march across the workers in pid order, with
    only a few computing at any instant. The chunks are about 83 MB in
    A and 35 MB in B. The original benchmark noted the same pattern.
    mirai's dispatcher streams tasks and mizu's workers read their
    claimed elements straight off shared pages, so neither shows idle
    workers.

[^sysr]: During mirai's D runs, the main process spent
    `r fmt(sysr("boot_pred_interval", "mirai"), 1)` kernel CPU-seconds
    per wall-clock second: socket writes, plus the macOS memory
    compressor working on worker heaps that retain task payloads.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Per-worker detail (13 grids)

```{r}
#| label: cpu-detail
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| results: asis

detail <- function(wl, be) {
  d <- mon |>
    filter(workload == wl_label[[wl]], backend == backend_label[[be]]) |>
    mutate(worker = factor(pid))
  if (nrow(d) == 0L) {
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }
  ggplot(d, aes(rel_time, pct_cpu, col = worker)) +
    geom_point(cex = 1 / 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1 / 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
    facet_wrap(~worker) +
    labs(
      title = paste(wl_label[[wl]], "—", backend_label[[be]]),
      x = "seconds", y = "CPU (%)"
    )
}

for (wl in names(wl_label)) {
  bes <- if (wl == "boot_pred_interval") {
    c("future", "mirai", "mizu", "mizu_stream")
  } else {
    c("future", "mirai", "mizu")
  }
  for (be in bes) {
    print(detail(wl, be))
  }
}
```
:::

## Findings

```{r}
#| label: findings-data
#| include: false

sp <- function(wl, be) get_speedup(wl, be)
el <- function(wl, be) get_elapsed(wl, be)
```

Per workload, fastest first:

- **A: Bootstrap metrics** (5,000 tasks of ~3 ms). Overhead-bound:
  there is little compute to split. mizu
  `r fmt(sp("boot_metrics", "mizu"), 1)`×
  (`r fmt(el("boot_metrics", "mizu"), 1)` s), mirai
  `r fmt(sp("boot_metrics", "mirai"), 1)`×, future
  `r fmt(sp("boot_metrics", "future"), 1)`×.
- **B: Resampled model fits** (250 tasks of ~45 ms). mizu
  `r fmt(sp("resample_fit", "mizu"), 1)`×, mirai
  `r fmt(sp("resample_fit", "mirai"), 1)`×, future
  `r fmt(sp("resample_fit", "future"), 1)`×.
- **C: Permutation importance** (240 replicates of ~85 ms, ~2.8 MB of
  data each). mizu `r fmt(sp("perm_importance", "mizu"), 1)`×
  (`r fmt(el("perm_importance", "mizu"), 1)` s), mirai
  `r fmt(sp("perm_importance", "mirai"), 1)`×, future
  `r fmt(sp("perm_importance", "future"), 1)`×.
- **D: Bootstrap prediction intervals** (400 refits, each scoring
  250,000 policies and returning 2 MB of predictions). mizu's streaming
  map is fastest by far: `r fmt(sp("boot_pred_interval", "mizu_stream"), 1)`×
  (`r fmt(el("boot_pred_interval", "mizu_stream"), 1)` s). The standard
  mizu map reaches `r fmt(sp("boot_pred_interval", "mizu"), 1)`×
  (`r fmt(el("boot_pred_interval", "mizu"), 1)` s), mirai
  `r fmt(sp("boot_pred_interval", "mirai"), 1)`×, and future
  `r fmt(sp("boot_pred_interval", "future"), 1)`×.[^everywhere]

The pattern across A to D: the gap between mizu and the socket-based
backends widens as data movement grows relative to compute. Larger
task inputs (A, B), a large shared input (D), and large results (D)
each add copying that mizu does once or not at all.

[^everywhere]: D's mirai number uses the standard calling convention,
    which re-sends the constant portfolio with every task. mirai's
    documented pattern for large shared objects is `everywhere()`: one
    export per worker, persisted across calls. Measured on D: a
    `r fmt(meta$extras$boot_pred_interval$export, 2)` s export, then
    `r fmt(meta$extras$boot_pred_interval$map, 1)` s per map. This is
    faster than the standard mizu map but not the streaming one, so
    D's ranking reflects the calling convention, not mirai's ceiling.
    On C the same pattern saves nothing, because the shared model is
    only 0.2 MB (export `r fmt(meta$extras$perm_importance$export, 2)`
    s, map `r fmt(meta$extras$perm_importance$map, 1)` s).

## Recommendations

For tidymodels users choosing a backend today:

- **mirai is the safe default.** It is on CRAN, it needs no size-limit
  settings, and it scales well from about 8 workers up.
- **mizu is the fastest option measured**, on every workload, and by
  the widest margin exactly where real modeling work moves the most
  data. It is not yet on CRAN.
- **future** remains a reasonable choice when tasks carry little data.
  Watch for the chunk dispatch stall on data-heavy workloads, and for
  the globals size limit on older versions.[^future-globals]

Two habits help on every backend. Strip fitted models to their
prediction essentials before sending them to workers.[^payload] And
set the RNG kind explicitly inside a task function if you compare
results across backends.[^rng]

[^future-globals]: future before 1.40.0 (April 2025) capped the
    globals exported to a multisession worker at 500 MiB per future by
    default, and aborted above it with *"Will not launch future due to
    the size of the globals …"*. Raising
    `options(future.globals.maxSize)` was a required extra step for
    large-payload workloads, one the other backends never needed.
    Since 1.40.0 the multisession backend defaults to no limit, and
    1.75.0 made `+Inf` the default on every code path. The
    `options(future.globals.maxSize = 8 * 1024^3)` in `benchmark.R` is
    a harmless remnant of that era.

[^payload]: The benchmark's fitted models are stripped butcher-style:
    no QR matrix, no model frame, no embedded data. An earlier
    revision of workload C shipped an unstripped glm (~300 MB) as a
    per-task constant. mirai then moved ~85 GB per run, and macOS
    repeatedly killed the session. Stripped fits benefit all three
    backends equally and are standard practice when deploying a model
    to workers.

[^rng]: mirai workers default to the L'Ecuyer-CMRG RNG, while R
    sessions default to Mersenne-Twister. A bare `set.seed()` inside a
    task then produces a *different* stream on mirai than on the other
    backends. Workload C pins `kind = "Mersenne-Twister"` to keep the
    results comparable.

## Reproducing

```sh
Rscript benchmark.R                # ~25 min; writes results/*.rds
bash run_all.sh                    # same, but one process per workload with
                                   # per-phase resume (robust to interruption)
BENCH_SWEEP=1 Rscript benchmark.R  # worker-count sweep for B and C;
                                   # writes results/sweep.rds
quarto render benchmark.qmd        # this report
```

Package versions at run time:

```{r}
#| label: versions

tibble(
  package = names(meta$packages),
  version = unname(meta$packages)
) |>
  knitr::kable()
```
